findings_initial.title: request_reset takes a visibly different amount of time for registered vs. unregistered emails
findings_initial.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: response to a reset request must not let an attacker distinguish registered from unregistered accounts, including via response-time side channels — the code path for both cases should take comparable time.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py request_reset(): for an unknown email it returns immediately (dict lookup only); for a known email it additionally calls new_token(), writes to self._resets, formats the link and calls mailer.send(). The comment says 'Don't reveal whether an email is registered' but only suppresses the response value, not the timing.
findings_initial.failure: An attacker can enumerate valid customer emails by measuring response latency of the forgot-password endpoint, enabling targeted credential-stuffing or phishing campaigns against confirmed accounts.

findings_initial.title: Older outstanding reset tokens for an account stay valid after a newer one is issued or after a reset already succeeds
findings_initial.requirement: Password-reset token lifecycle best practice (OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet / NIST 800-63B): issuing a new reset token or completing a reset should invalidate all other outstanding tokens for that account, since each represents a live credential.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py request_reset() always adds a new token to self._resets without removing/expiring any prior token for the same email; reset_password() only deletes the single token it consumed, leaving any other still-live token for that account usable.
findings_initial.failure: If an older reset email is intercepted, cached, or forwarded (e.g., via a compromised mailbox or shared inbox) after the legitimate user has already requested a newer link or already reset their password, the old token remains a valid, unused credential for up to 15 minutes — allowing account takeover after the rightful owner believes the account is secured.

findings_initial.title: reset_password has a check-then-act race that lets a single token be consumed more than once under concurrent requests
findings_initial.requirement: Single-use token invariant for password-reset tokens: a token must be consumable at most once, even under concurrent/duplicate submissions (this is the standard 'at-most-once' guarantee expected of any one-time credential, analogous to OAuth authorization codes).
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py reset_password(): the token is looked up (self._resets.get), validated, and only deleted from self._resets after the password hash is written — there is no lock or atomic pop, so two concurrent calls with the same token can both pass validation before either deletion happens.
findings_initial.failure: Under a real multi-threaded/async account service, two near-simultaneous submissions of the same reset link (e.g., a user double-clicking, or a browser retry after a slow response) — or a race with an attacker replaying an intercepted link — can both 'succeed', producing a nondeterministic final password and violating the single-use contract the rest of the system relies on.

findings_initial.title: reset_password accepts any new_password, including empty string
findings_initial.requirement: NIST SP 800-63B / OWASP ASVS minimum password requirements (e.g., non-empty, minimum length) that any credential-setting endpoint — signup or reset — must enforce equally, so the reset path can't be used to bypass whatever policy exists elsewhere.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py reset_password() passes new_password directly to hash_password() with no length or emptiness check.
findings_initial.failure: A user (or attacker who obtains a valid token) can set the account password to an empty string or a trivially weak value, silently downgrading account security below whatever bar the normal signup flow enforces.

findings_initial.title: request_reset has no throttling, so it can be called unlimited times for the same email
findings_initial.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet requirement to rate-limit reset requests per account/IP to prevent abuse (email bombing) and to bound resource consumption.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py request_reset() unconditionally generates a token and sends mail on every call with no counter, cooldown, or per-email/per-IP limit.
findings_initial.failure: An attacker can flood a victim's inbox with reset emails (harassment/DoS against the user) or repeatedly hit the mail-sending path to exhaust downstream mail-service quota, with no code-level defense.

findings_initial.title: Expired or unused tokens are only ever removed from _resets when they happen to be looked up again
findings_initial.requirement: Lifecycle management for time-bounded state: expired tokens must be purged (via TTL sweep or lazy cleanup on every relevant path) so stored state doesn't grow unbounded for the life of the process.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py: self._resets entries are deleted only inside reset_password() on expiry/success/missing-user paths. A token that is requested but never redeemed (the common case for the ~4/week manual resets this feature replaces, times any abuse volume) stays in the dict forever, since nothing sweeps it after expiry.
findings_initial.failure: Combined with the lack of rate limiting, repeated reset requests accumulate permanently in memory for the lifetime of the process, giving an attacker (or just normal usage over time) an easy unbounded-memory-growth vector against the account service.

findings_final.title: A valid, unexpired reset token is permanently destroyed on a recoverable validation failure (password too short)
findings_final.requirement: Forgot-password flow contract in the ticket: 'They click it and set a new password.' A reset link is expected to remain usable until it is successfully consumed or expires — OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet treats the token as single-use only on a *successful* password change, not on client-side input validation failures.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py reset_password() calls `self._resets.pop(token, None)` unconditionally before checking `len(new_password) < self.MIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH`. Verified live: calling reset_password(token, 'short') returns False as expected, but a second call with the *same* token and a strong password also returns False and the password is never changed — the token was consumed by the first, failed attempt.
findings_final.failure: A user who mistypes or picks a too-short password on their first try permanently loses their reset link. The form can't just show a validation error and let them retry — they are silently locked out and must go back to 'forgot password' and wait out the request cooldown for an entirely new email. This will generate exactly the kind of support tickets ACT-412 was meant to eliminate.

findings_final.title: Reset tokens are stored as plaintext bearer credentials in the service's token store
findings_final.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: the reset token should be stored server-side only in hashed form (like a password or session token), precisely because it is a bearer credential that grants account takeover if disclosed.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py: `self._resets: dict[str, tuple[str, float]]` is keyed by the raw token returned by new_token(), and reset_password() does `self._resets.pop(token, None)` directly against the plaintext value — no hash of the token is stored or compared.
findings_final.failure: Any compromise of the process's memory, a debug/error log that captures the token dict, or a backup/snapshot of this store hands an attacker fully-usable password-reset credentials for every outstanding request, with no additional verification step required.

findings_final.title: Request cooldown is only enforced for registered emails, so requests against unregistered addresses are never rate-limited
findings_final.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet requires rate-limiting of the reset-request endpoint regardless of whether the target account exists, both to prevent resource-exhaustion abuse and to avoid the throttle itself becoming a side channel for enumerating valid accounts.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py request_reset(): `if user is None: return` happens *before* the `_last_request` cooldown check/update, so `self._last_request` is never populated for unknown emails and the cooldown branch is unreachable for them — every call regenerates a token and re-does full expiry/link work with no throttling.
findings_final.failure: An attacker can invoke request_reset for an unlimited number of non-existent addresses with no backoff, while real accounts are throttled to one email per 60s — a distinguishable behavioral asymmetry that can be used as part of an account-enumeration oracle, and a free amplification vector for wasting CPU/entropy on token generation at unlimited rate.

findings_final.title: Concurrent request_reset calls for the same email can invalidate a token that was already emailed to the user
findings_final.requirement: Check-then-act sequences (cooldown check, token invalidation, token store write, last-request write) that mutate shared state must be atomic under concurrent access for the service to behave correctly when called from multiple workers/threads or a double-submitted form — a property implied by the multi-worker deployment any production account service runs under.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py request_reset(): the cooldown read (`self._last_request.get(email)`), `_invalidate_tokens_for(email)`, and the writes to `self._resets`/`self._last_request` are not guarded by any lock. Verified: after two interleaved calls that both observe stale cooldown state, both emails are sent (mailer.sent length 2) but the first call's token is removed from `self._resets` by the second call's `_invalidate_tokens_for`, before it could ever be used.
findings_final.failure: A user who double-clicks 'send reset link', or whose request hits two different app-server workers in a race, receives two reset emails where the first is already dead on arrival — they click the first (most recently received, if their mail client reorders) link and get a confusing 'invalid or expired token' error despite having just received it.

findings_final.title: Email lookup for reset requests is case-sensitive, unlike normal email semantics
findings_final.requirement: RFC 5321/5322 treats the domain part of an email address as case-insensitive, and virtually every real mail and auth system in practice also treats the local part case-insensitively for account matching; users routinely type their address with different casing than at signup.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py request_reset(): `user = self.users.get(email)` is a raw dict lookup with no normalization. Verified: a user stored as 'Ada@Example.com' gets zero emails sent when requesting a reset as 'ada@example.com'.
findings_final.failure: A legitimate, registered user who types their email in different case than it was stored gets no error and no email — indistinguishable (by design, for enumeration-resistance) from submitting an unregistered address, so they conclude the self-service flow is broken and go back to emailing support, defeating the point of the ticket.

findings_initial.title: No mutual exclusion for two concurrent requests carrying the same idempotency key
findings_initial.requirement: Idempotency-key semantics (as implemented by Stripe and other payment APIs) require that a request with a key already 'in flight' be rejected or blocked (typically a 409 'request in progress') rather than allowed to proceed to the processor a second time. This is the exact 'two attempts at once' case the feature exists to close.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge: `record = self._idempotency_keys.get(idempotency_key)` is read, then `_execute` is called, then the record is written -- a classic check-then-act gap. Nothing marks the key as 'in progress' before `_execute` runs, so two requests that arrive close together (e.g. the mobile client's automatic retry firing before the first response returns -- the scenario the ticket itself describes) both find no record, both call `_execute`, and both append to `self.executed`.
findings_initial.failure: A customer is charged twice from two nearly-simultaneous requests carrying the identical idempotency key -- precisely the double-charge support ticket this feature was built to eliminate, just moved from 'sequential retry' to 'concurrent retry'.

findings_initial.title: A transient processor failure (5xx) is cached and permanently returned to all future retries with that key
findings_initial.requirement: Documented idempotency-key behavior (Stripe API) explicitly does not persist an idempotent result for a request that resulted in a 500-range/processor error; such failures are meant to be safely retryable with the same key. Only completed, deterministic results (2xx, or a definitive 4xx) should be locked in.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge caches whatever `_execute` returns unconditionally: `self._idempotency_keys[idempotency_key] = {"status": status, "body": body, ...}` runs the same way whether status is 200 or 500. Verified: after a first attempt with `simulate="processor_down"` returns 500, a later retry with the same key and corrected params returns 409 ('different parameters') because the failed attempt's params (including the stale `simulate` flag) are frozen in the record -- there is no way to ever successfully charge with that key again.
findings_initial.failure: After any transient upstream outage, the client is permanently stuck: retrying with the same key returns the cached failure forever, and retrying with different/corrected params returns a 409. The only escape is generating a brand-new idempotency key, which the client has no way of knowing it needs to do -- this converts one class of support ticket (double charge) into another (payment permanently stuck / customer can't be charged even when the processor has recovered).

findings_initial.title: Idempotency records never expire and the store grows unboundedly
findings_initial.requirement: Published idempotency-key specs (Stripe: 24-hour key lifetime) bound how long a key is honored, both to allow legitimate key reuse after the window and to bound server-side storage. The ticket's explicit instruction to source time from the injected `Clock` (not `time.time()`) is a strong signal that time-based expiry was expected.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py stores `"at": self.clock.now()` on every record but never reads it back anywhere -- there is no expiry check in `post_charge`, and `self._idempotency_keys` is a plain dict with no eviction.
findings_initial.failure: In production this dict is process-lifetime, unbounded, and keyed by client-supplied strings -- an ever-growing memory leak, and legitimate key reuse after a reasonable window (e.g. a customer paying again a week later using an SDK that reuses UUIDs from a pool) is permanently blocked with a 409 instead of being allowed to proceed as a fresh charge.

findings_initial.title: If the upstream call raises instead of returning, the idempotency record is never written and a retry re-charges
findings_initial.requirement: The ticket's own invariant: 'self.executed is the ledger of what the upstream processor actually attempted. One entry = money moved once' implies that any code path where `_execute` has been entered (and thus may have moved money) must be captured by the idempotency layer before it can be retried.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge calls `status, body = self._execute(params)` with no try/except; the idempotency dict is only populated in the lines immediately after that call returns normally. `_execute` explicitly documents that once entered, 'the attempt is on the ledger whether or not it succeeded' -- i.e. it's expected to be able to fail/throw for reasons other than a clean 500 (e.g. a network exception talking to the real processor). Any such exception unwinds `post_charge` with no idempotency record persisted.
findings_initial.failure: A network-level failure between the service and the real payment processor (the single most common failure mode for a payments integration) leaves an entry in `self.executed` (money may have moved) but no idempotency record. The client's automatic retry with the same key then sees no record, calls `_execute` again, and the customer is charged twice.

findings_initial.title: Idempotency records live only in process memory and are lost on restart/deploy
findings_initial.requirement: A payments idempotency guarantee must survive the process that handled the original request, since deploys, autoscaling, and crashes routinely rotate the process/instance that a retry lands on.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py: `self._idempotency_keys: dict[str, dict] = {}` is an instance attribute of `ChargeAPI` with no persistence layer; nothing here writes the record anywhere durable.
findings_initial.failure: A deploy or worker restart between the original charge and the client's retry (a very plausible window, since the ticket describes retries triggered by dropped connections) wipes the idempotency table; the retry lands on a fresh process with no memory of the key and charges the customer again -- the same failure class the feature is meant to close.

findings_initial.title: An empty-string idempotency key is accepted and treated as a real, distinct key
findings_initial.requirement: Boundary handling for a client-supplied identifier: an empty string is not a meaningful idempotency key and should be treated the same as 'no key supplied' (or rejected), not silently accepted as valid deduplication state.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py checks `if idempotency_key is not None`, so `idempotency_key=""` passes the guard and is used as a real dict key in `self._idempotency_keys`.
findings_initial.failure: A client bug that sends `""` instead of omitting the header gets silent, unintended deduplication behavior (or a spurious 409 on the next such request) instead of a clear validation error, making the failure mode hard to diagnose.

findings_final.title: On a mid-charge exception the idempotency key is deleted and a retry starts a brand-new, unprotected attempt
findings_final.requirement: Idempotency-key semantics for payment APIs (the model this ticket follows, e.g. Stripe's Idempotent Requests): when the outcome of contacting the processor is unknown (timeout / connection drop / crash), the key must NOT be treated as free-for-reuse, because the underlying charge may have already succeeded. Only requests that are known to have produced no side effect may be safely retried as brand-new.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py:84-91 calls self.before_execute() -- documented as the extension point Ops uses to 'inject latency and to replay traffic', i.e. simulate exactly the network conditions the ticket describes -- BEFORE appending to self.executed. If before_execute (or anything before line 91) raises, the except block at 132-140 pops the idempotency key and re-raises, with no record in self.executed and no memory that this key was ever attempted.
findings_final.failure: The exact scenario in the ticket -- the client's connection drops during a charge and the SDK auto-retries -- maps to precisely this code path when the drop happens on our side talking to the processor. Because the key is deleted, the retry is treated as a fresh charge and calls _execute again. If the original attempt actually reached and was processed by the processor before the exception was raised, the customer is billed twice, and self.executed only shows one entry, so the ledger the ticket asks engineers to trust hides the double charge.

findings_final.title: A key claimed 'in_progress' has no timeout and is never released if the process dies or before_execute hangs
findings_final.requirement: An idempotency lock must have a bounded lifetime independent of the 24h key TTL; the TTL check for the record is only run for records whose status != 'in_progress'.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py:109-112 gates the TTL expiry check on record['status'] != 'in_progress', and 113-117 returns 409 whenever status == 'in_progress'. The only code paths that ever clear an in_progress record are the success path (142-154) and the exception path (137-139) of the SAME call that created it -- there is no independent lock timeout.
findings_final.failure: If the process is killed mid-charge (OOM, deploy, orchestrator restart) -- explicitly a supported case per the docstring recommending a durable MutableMapping 'to survive process restarts/deploys' -- the in_progress record survives the restart with nothing left to clear it. Every subsequent request with that idempotency key gets a permanent 409 forever, even after the 24h window the ticket relies on for key reuse. The customer can never complete that charge with that key and support has no self-service recovery path.

findings_final.title: Comment claims the 24h TTL 'bounds storage', but expired records are only evicted lazily on exact-key lookup
findings_final.requirement: A stated storage-bounding mechanism must actually bound storage; otherwise the durable store (which the docstring explicitly recommends for production use) grows without limit.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py:15-17 comment: 'Stripe-style 24h idempotency key lifetime: bounds storage'. But the only eviction logic (lines 109-112) runs inside post_charge and only fires when that specific key is looked up again after expiry. Keys that are used once and never retried are never removed.
findings_final.failure: In production, most idempotency keys are used exactly once and never looked up again. With no background sweep, the durable store (shelve/disk-backed, per the class docstring's own recommendation) grows unbounded with every charge ever made, contradicting the stated bounding rationale and eventually causing disk/memory exhaustion or unbounded cost on the backing store.

findings_final.title: idempotency_key accepts any string with no length or character validation
findings_final.requirement: Published idempotency-key contracts (e.g. Stripe limits keys to 255 characters) bound key size specifically to prevent unbounded storage/log growth per request.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py:104, `key = idempotency_key or None`, is the only normalization applied to the incoming key before it is used as a dict key and stored verbatim in `_idempotency_keys` (line 125-130 / 149-154), with `params` and `body` copied alongside it.
findings_final.failure: A malformed or malicious client can send an arbitrarily large string as the idempotency key on every request; each becomes a permanent (until TTL-lookup-eviction, which per the prior finding may never happen) entry in the store, including a durable on-disk store, giving an attacker or buggy client a cheap way to inflate storage and degrade the service.

findings_initial.title: Only comma-delimited CSV is accepted; semicolon-delimited exports fail entirely
findings_initial.requirement: Ticket states 'The files come from the customer's own systems — HR exports, spreadsheets, whatever they've got — so we don't control how they're produced.' A large share of Excel exports in non-US locales (most of Europe) default to semicolon as the field separator because comma is the decimal separator. RFC 4180 itself doesn't mandate comma, and real-world CSV producers vary.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:43 hardcodes `csv.reader(io.StringIO(text))` with no dialect sniffing (e.g. `csv.Sniffer`). Verified: `import_users('email;name;team\nada@example.com;...')` returns zero users and the error 'Missing required column(s): email, name, team' — the entire file is rejected, not just malformed rows.
findings_initial.failure: An admin uploading a perfectly valid export from a European customer's HR system gets a total failure with a misleading 'missing column' error, even though the columns are right there separated by semicolons. This directly contradicts the ticket's premise that varied customer-produced files must be handled.

findings_initial.title: Duplicate column names in the header silently overwrite each other with no error
findings_initial.requirement: Contract states result.users must be 'keyed by the header column names' and that unimportable rows must be reported in errors — implicit requirement that data isn't silently lost or misattributed when it can't be unambiguously mapped.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:69 builds the record via `zip(header, row)` into a plain dict. Verified: header `email,name,team,email` with row `a@x.com,Ada,Eng,a2@x.com` produces a single user with email `a2@x.com` — the first email column's value is silently discarded and no error or warning is emitted.
findings_initial.failure: If a customer's export has a duplicate or renamed-but-colliding column (common in hand-edited HR spreadsheets, e.g. two 'email' columns for personal/work), the importer picks whichever comes last and never tells the admin data was dropped, potentially importing the wrong email address for a user account.

findings_initial.title: Duplicate emails within the same file are imported as separate users with no error
findings_initial.requirement: Ticket: 'Rows that can't be imported get reported back to the admin.' A row creating a user with an email already claimed by another row in the same batch cannot be validly imported as a distinct account and should be flagged, since email is presumably the unique identifier for a user record.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py has no dedup/uniqueness check across rows. Verified: two rows with `a@x.com` both pass through into `result.users` with no error.
findings_initial.failure: The admin UI/downstream user-creation step receives two 'create user' records for the same email; depending on how that layer handles conflicts, the second either silently overwrites the first, errors out for reasons the admin never sees explained here, or creates inconsistent state — none of which is surfaced back through the reported errors this feature promises.

findings_initial.title: Required-column check is case-sensitive and only trims outer whitespace
findings_initial.requirement: Ticket premise: files are customer-produced and uncontrolled ('whatever they've got'). A bulk import that must tolerate arbitrary customer formatting should not fail solely because a header cell reads 'Email' instead of 'email'.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:50-56 strips whitespace but does no case normalization before comparing against REQUIRED_COLUMNS. Verified: header `Email,Name,Team` triggers 'Missing required column(s): email, name, team' even though all three columns are present under different casing.
findings_initial.failure: A customer's HR export with Title-Case or ALL-CAPS headers (extremely common) is rejected outright with zero rows imported, forcing the admin to manually edit the source file before every upload — defeating the purpose of accepting arbitrary customer exports.

findings_initial.title: No limit on row count or file size before processing
findings_initial.requirement: General availability/robustness expectation for an admin-facing file upload endpoint accepting externally-produced files: unbounded input must not be able to exhaust server resources on a single request.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py reads the entire csv_text into memory (io.StringIO) and iterates every row into result.users/result.errors with no cap on row count or total size.
findings_initial.failure: An oversized or malformed file (accidentally or intentionally, e.g. a multi-GB export or a file with millions of blank-looking rows) is processed in full in one request, risking memory exhaustion or a hung request on the admin service — a low-effort denial-of-service vector for a feature explicitly built to accept files the team does not control.

findings_final.title: Email column is only checked for non-emptiness, never validated as an email
findings_final.requirement: A bulk user-import feature that reports 'rows that can't be imported' must validate the semantic correctness of the identifying field (RFC 5321/5322 email syntax), not just its presence — otherwise garbage values silently become account identifiers.
findings_final.evidence: app/importer.py: the only check on `record['email']` is `empty_required` (non-blank). Verified: `import_users('email,name,team\nnot-an-email,Bob,Eng\n')` returns the row in `result.users` with `email: 'not-an-email'` and no error.
findings_final.failure: Any garbage string in the email column (typos, 'N/A', a name pasted into the wrong column) becomes a user record with an invalid email and is silently accepted instead of being reported to the admin. Downstream invite/notification emails will bounce or never send, and the admin has no signal from the import that anything was wrong.

findings_final.title: Untrusted cell values starting with =, +, -, @ are passed through unsanitized into user records
findings_final.requirement: OWASP CSV Injection / Formula Injection guidance (CWE-1236): data originating from an untrusted, customer-controlled file that may later be opened in Excel/Sheets or re-exported as CSV must have leading formula-trigger characters neutralized or flagged, since spreadsheet applications execute cell content beginning with =, +, -, or @.
findings_final.evidence: app/importer.py builds `record` via a straight `.strip()` of each cell with no sanitization; verified `import_users('email,name,team,notes\nada@example.com,Ada,Eng,=cmd|/c calc!A0\n')` returns the formula string unmodified in `result.users[0]['notes']`. The ticket explicitly states 'any other columns come through as-is' from files the team does not control.
findings_final.failure: If an admin exports the resulting user list back to CSV/Excel for review (a common admin-UI action), a malicious or corrupted customer export can trigger arbitrary formula execution (including OS command execution via DDE/cmd formulas) on the admin's machine — a well-known, actively exploited attack class. A security reviewer would block sign-off on this under CWE-1236.

findings_final.title: Reported error line numbers are wrong once any earlier row contains a quoted multi-line field
findings_final.requirement: Error messages returned to the admin must reference the actual physical line in the uploaded file (a basic usability/correctness requirement for 'rows that can't be imported get reported back to the admin') so the admin can locate and fix the bad row.
findings_final.evidence: app/importer.py uses `enumerate(reader, start=2)`, counting *logical CSV rows*, not physical file lines. Verified: with a valid row containing an RFC-4180 quoted embedded newline (physical lines 2-3), the next bad row is on physical line 4 but is reported as 'Row 3'.
findings_final.failure: Admins with legitimately quoted multi-line fields (e.g. addresses, notes) get error messages pointing at the wrong line, making it harder to locate and fix bad rows in larger files, increasing support burden.
